executive_summary: The defining thread running through today's content is the intensifying struggle over who controls transformative technology — and on whose terms. The Musk v. Altman trial, as covered in MIT Technology Review, has stripped away legal complexity to expose a raw power contest: two men with competing visions for governing artificial general intelligence, with a jury now tasked with deciding not just a lawsuit but a legitimacy question that will echo across Silicon Valley. Google's precarious position at I/O 2026 — third in foundation models, playing catch-up on coding while clinging to a lead in scientific AI — reinforces that this governance vacuum is unfolding amid a genuinely unsettled competitive landscape, where no single actor has consolidated dominance. The Economist's examination of the backlash against data centres adds a further dimension: the physical infrastructure enabling this AI race is itself becoming a contested resource, drawing public resistance and regulatory scrutiny even as demand accelerates. Taken together, these stories describe a single, consequential moment in which the rules, the winners, and the costs of the AI era are all simultaneously up for grabs — and the institutions capable of arbitrating those questions, from courtrooms to regulatory bodies, are visibly straining under the weight.

newsletters.title: 🔴 Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?

items.headline: Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?
items.blurb: A year ago I reported on the impact of artificial intelligence on the fight against climate change. On the one hand, data centres used a lot of electricity; on the other, that electricity was mostly renewable, and could be used to develop technologies that helped cut emissions around the world. Overall it felt like cause for cautious optimism, especially if—as we argued in an accompanying leader—AI companies would share more information about the impact of their systems to help consumers make informed decisions. A lot has changed since then. Some shifts were predictable. The amount of electricity the AI industry uses has exploded. The biggest models take more energy to train and run than they did last year, and they are being used by more people to do more things more of the time. Some adjustments were grimly inevitable. Where big tech companies once felt bound by promises they had made in a different political era to cut, or even reverse, their emissions, they now seem happy to switch on new gas turbines to power their growing ambitions, although they still generally insist that the extra energy use is just a temporary measure to compensate for a lack of capacity on the electricity grid. Other changes were more surprising. Last year data-centre impacts felt like a niche topic discussed by people interested in the overlap between AI and climate change. Now they are an increasingly important part of national—and international—politics. In America politicians are proposing regional and national moratoriums on construction, prompting entrepreneurs to wonder whether it might be cheaper to launch computers into space rather than fight through the morass on Earth.

longform.title: Musk v. Altman week 3: now the jury will pick a side
longform.thesis: The final week of the Musk v. Altman trial reduced to a credibility contest between two men, with Altman accused of lying and self-dealing and Musk portrayed as a power-seeker bent on controlling AGI, leaving the jury to adjudicate not just legal claims but competing narratives about who should govern transformative AI.
longform.context: MIT Technology Review reporter Michelle Kim, who is also a lawyer, covered all three weeks of the Musk v. Altman trial from the courtroom; this newsletter dispatch summarizes the explosive closing week as the case moved toward jury deliberation in May 2026.
arguments: Both sides concentrated their closing arguments on personal discrediting: Altman's lawyers alleged he lied and engaged in self-dealing regarding OpenAI's nonprofit status and assets, while Musk's legal team was countered with the portrayal of Musk as a 'power-seeker trying to control artificial general intelligence' rather than a principled objector.

The trial surfaced new documentary and testimonial detail about OpenAI's contested nonprofit-to-for-profit conversion, suggesting the legal dispute is as much about the governance and ownership of frontier AI as it is about the original founding agreements between the two men.

A symbolic detail — a golden trophy of a donkey's ass awarded to an employee who challenged Musk — was entered into or emerged from the proceedings, illustrating the toxic internal culture claims that underscore the broader power struggle narrative both sides are constructing for the jury.
longform.significance: The case forces a public, adversarial examination of how AGI-era companies should be governed and whether nonprofit mission commitments can be legally enforced against billionaire founders — questions no prior litigation has tested at this scale. A jury verdict either way will set a precedent shaping how AI labs structure their missions and ownership, and will publicly legitimize or delegitimize one of the two most influential figures in commercial AI development.
questions_raised: Whether a lay jury can meaningfully adjudicate competing expert framings of what OpenAI's founding documents actually obligated the parties to do with respect to AGI safety and nonprofit assets.

If Musk loses, whether the verdict forecloses his broader legal and regulatory campaign against OpenAI's for-profit conversion, or whether parallel regulatory challenges in state attorneys-general offices remain viable.

longform.title: What to expect from Google this week
longform.thesis: Google enters I/O 2026 as a clear third-place foundation model competitor, with a critical coding deficit against Anthropic and OpenAI, but retains a meaningful lead in AI for science that the conference may reinforce.
longform.context: Written as a preview dispatch ahead of Google I/O 2026, this piece responds to a year-long shift in the competitive AI landscape in which Google's Gemini models lost parity with rivals, particularly in coding, forcing some DeepMind engineers to use Anthropic's Claude Code for their own work.
arguments: Google has fallen to third place in the foundation model race primarily because its coding tools have been 'outgunned' by Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex — a deficit so acute that DeepMind engineers were reportedly fighting over Claude Code access as recently as a month before I/O, making a full comeback at the conference unlikely despite a new dedicated coding team and Nobel laureate John Jumper's involvement.

Science and health AI represent Google's genuine competitive advantage: as 'the only frontier AI company to have earned a Nobel Prize,' Google has solidified its lead in AI-for-science as LLMs have come to dominate that landscape, with tools like the AI co-scientist (described as an 'oracle' by a Stanford scientist) and AlphaEvolve already deployed — making any new scientific announcements at I/O consequentially underreported relative to the coding narrative.

Google's health AI ambitions are ambiguous: the company leads in LLM-based health research but has ceded the consumer health AI conversation to OpenAI since ChatGPT Health launched in January 2025, and its forthcoming Health Coach appears oriented toward fitness and diet advice rather than clinical concerns — raising the unresolved question of whether this represents strategic caution or competitive lag.

Google faces internal and reputational political pressure that could disrupt I/O's messaging: 600 employees, many from DeepMind, protested a Department of Defense deal the day before Google signed it, and while CEO Demis Hassabis has avoided the public CEO feuds defining the broader AI industry, 'controversies will worm their way in regardless' of Google's effort to 'maintain its veneer of neutrality.'
longform.significance: This piece matters as a real-time diagnostic of competitive stratification within frontier AI, illustrating that leadership is now domain-specific — coding versus science — rather than monolithic. It challenges the narrative of Google as a default AI frontrunner and surfaces an underexamined tension between Google DeepMind's scientific credibility and its failure to translate that credibility into product dominance. The framing of health AI as either 'appropriate caution' or competitive retreat is a live policy and commercial question with stakes beyond the conference.
questions_raised: Is Google's restrained approach to consumer health AI — fitness and diet coaching rather than clinical guidance — a principled risk-management decision or evidence that it has genuinely fallen behind OpenAI in defining the health AI category?

Can Google's scientific AI leadership (Nobel Prize, AlphaFold, AlphaEvolve) translate into a durable competitive moat if its foundation models continue to lag in coding, the benchmark increasingly used to rank overall model capability?
